en: Preparing an army like forty nobles,
She raided Ombu and took ten.
He attacked Seytek.
She took a thousand black-eyed ones,
And took gold coins loaded on elephants.
Gathering forty-two hosts of troops,
For forty-two hosts of people
She gathered many coats of gold.
She made her mighty Manas khan,
And made him a man of sacred virtue.
In the Beijing of Kakan Khan,
She made Manas khan for six months.
'Kanykey, the people's leader,
How could she do such a thing?
Without shame, men's clothes—
With what face could she wear them?
How could Kanykey
Lead her aged horse,
Saying, "I shall race him"?' you say."
Unable to die of shame,
Unable to take his own life,
Khan Temir's golden throne,
With a plane-tree garden in its midst—
If soaked in water forty years,
Not the slightest edge would fade;
If soaked for eighty years,
It would not loosen and rot.
Of gold-patterned carpets,
Sixty were spread out.
Of Temir Khan's tower,
Do not ask about the watch-post's splendor.
Hearing words from his wayward people,
Temir Khan was choked with emotion.
When he came out from the watch-post and looked,
His dear child Kanykey
Had tightly gathered her girth-thick hair,
And tied it upon her crown.
Her arrowproof armor,
She had put it all on together.
Her sword, axe, and spear
She had hung in their proper places.
Black-steel Zulpukor
She had fastened snugly at her wrist.
The double-edged Aktinte
She had drawn from its sheath.
She had dressed in men's clothes,
Trampling over the peoples of eight khans,
There went my child Kanykey.
Those who saw her were unsettled.
If you looked at each part of her body,
Her husband who had passed away,
Manas—how much she looked like him!
From her mouth, blue flame
Darted aside and hissed.
Her formidable teeth, like a gate,
Scattered like grains of millet.
Those who came straight before her
Split apart and scurried away,
Calling out greetings.
She had raised tremendous uproar.
"My foal, my child Kanykey,
Taytoru, sixty years of maturity,
You lead, saying, 'I shall race him.'
My foal, my child Kanykey,
God has blessed this fierce woman."
When he saw Kanykey,
Was Temir Khan not a khan?
Seeing the distress,
He was deeply grieved and ashamed.
"Since Kanykey has become like this,
Who would not become like this?" he said.
Waving his hands in anguish,
Offended with Kanykey, he said:
"Hey, Kanykey, my foal,
Turn your horse's head this way.
My honor is gone, Kanykey.
Stand here in front!
While your head is still upon your shoulders,
My foal, do not settle along the river.
Letting them call you a desperate woman—
Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Do not become the people's laughingstock!
You have no support to lean on,
My valiant child Kanykey.
To make your horse race more strongly,
To stand upon the ridge and shout,
Your renowned lion Manas is not here.
Saying, 'I shall race a horse,' Kanykey,
Do not go astray without cause.
Blustering, Kanykey,
Do not seek to count up heaps of gold.
Becoming a laughingstock to many khans,
My foal, do not race your Taytoru.
While your head is still upon your shoulders,
Do not settle along the river.
Letting them call you a desperate woman,
My dear Kanykey,
Do not become the people's laughingstock!
My child, you have no support to lean on,
No secure place of your own,
Who subdued every place he faced—
Those who opposed him,
He seized and broke them.
Your panther, lion Manas, is gone.
You have no grounds to enter a race.
To shout encouragement aloud,
Your fortunate Kyrgyz people are gone.
Living widowed, my foal,
Do not grow rash without cause.
O Kanykey, my foal,
My little one born to good fortune,
With eight hundred households in your hands,
Kanykey, have you suffered want of people?
You have all four kinds of livestock.
Kanykey, have you suffered want of wealth?
O Kanykey, my foal,
Driving wild sheep, panting,
From palm-sized Bukhara,
I myself, though I am khan,
Have entered four steeds; choose among them.
I myself entered Aktulpar.
Should Aktulpar come first,
Take the first prize yourself,
And take the horse along with it.
Shaatemir entered Chongkurong,
Ismayyl his Chongkashka,
Koloykan his Karakashka argamak.
Leave two and take one.
Whichever comes in first,
Take the horse and all the first prize.
May I come to no good if I dispute a horse with you!
If I dispute a prize with you,
O Kanykey, my foal,
May I no longer be a Muslim!
Like a post for tying horses,
May I be stripped bare!
Failing to know God's oneness,
My child, may I become an unbeliever!”
When her father called her a widow,
Your proud sister-in-law Kanykey—
How could she fail to feel shame?
We shall sell our coursers and pay tribute;
Parted from her Magnanimous One,
Your poor woman who lived in shame,
When her father called her a widow,
Unable to sniff back her running nose,
Unable to wipe her eyes,
With her very bones seeming to part,
Her tears streaming down,
Kanykey stood and said:
“The dear bird called the crane
You let the goshawk devour.
My dear soul steeped in grief,
When I fled to Bukhara,
You made my father call me a widow.
You let the hunting bird devour the swan.
My life falling into ruin,
You made my father call me a widow.
Wretched father, you have done no good!
You too insulted me as a widow.
My dear father,
Was this a gathering of multitudes?
In these cities, Samarkand and Bukhara,
Parted from all her people at once—
Was there no other widow like me?
Father, my dear father,
If you race Aktulpar and he wins,
When I, a bitch dying for wealth,
Take his first prize,
What wish would I fulfill?
Do not block my way, Father.
Let go of my hand, Father.
He was a horse granted by fortune.
Here in this Bukhara,
Let me race my Taytoru.
Who would love
A widow like me?
I shall try as an omen
My fleet horse Taytoru!
Taytoru, entered for the prize,
Was a renowned swift horse.
When my heroic lord died,
When this head met with suffering,
When Abyke, Kobosh, the six villains,
The vast wealth left by the Magnanimous One,
They shared it, measuring it out with whips.
When this head met with calamity,
He was a revered man,
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan:
He gave me this Taytoru as a mourning gift.
Counting his grown years,
He had reached sixty.
This very year, my Taytoru
Had reached sixty grown years.
If my bay comes in first,
I shall share his first prize.
If Taytoru falls behind,
Without letting you call me a widow,
I shall die before my appointed death!
While I have my argamak horse,
Father, I shall put no bridle on honor.
While my Magnanimous One and our Kyrgyz people's
Spirits watch over me,
I shall not sell my ancestral honor to the Sarts.
I shall not sit without racing my horse.
Gather your people of eight khans.
Restrain your foolish people.
If some wretch acts wickedly,
If he blocks my horse's way,
I shall not spare my life;
Today I shall spill my blood!
If anyone interferes with my horse,
I shall seize him on the road,
Drag him along the road,
And offer him as a sacrifice.
Whoever goes too far in villainy,
I shall cut off his head.
If my anger grows fierce,
I shall cut him up for the dogs!”
So saying then,
Her white whip with its black handle,
She grasped and swung it,
Making her bay cry out,
She drew it back against her thigh.
Making the face of the earth collapse,
Shouting, “Drive the horses!”
She galloped into Bukhara.
She shouted toward the lowlands;
Not one soul remained there.
When she shouted toward the mountains,
Not one soul remained there.
Shouting in anger,
All the multitude,
Your dear mother Kanykey
Drove in, scattering them before her.
The reason she drove them before her—
Dividing her back hair into ten,
Was she not your sister-in-law who braided it?
Greatness and sovereignty,
While your great lord lived—
Was she not your sister-in-law who knew them?
Manas Khan was her sovereign;
Had he not been a ruler?
To all the people, Kanykey,
While her sovereign lived—
Had she not been a mother?
At Khan Kokotoy's memorial feast,
At the head of the great assembly,
Of the hairy-mouthed Russians,
When their ten tribes came,
Of the red-tasseled Chinese,
When their forty tribes came,
When the people gathered,
When unbelievers and Muslims
Stood confronting each other,
She made all forty dignitaries
